title: ODT termination current recycled into the array supply rail
idea: Stack: keep 40-ohm on-die termination AND add zero I/O energy. Instead of terminating DQ lines to ground or VTT through a resistor, each ODT leg returns its current into the VARY array rail through a shunt-regulated low-impedance node, so incoming write traffic tops up the rail the sense amps drain anyway; a small shunt clamp dumps only the excess.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): termination is roughly a third of DDR5 write-path power; reusing it as array supply recovers about the VARY/VDDQ fraction (~40-50%) of that energy with no protocol change.

title: Gate-charge popcount on a sub-threshold wordline ramp flags silent flips
idea: Stack: catch every retention or hammer flip AND never open the row. The sub-wordline driver ramps a row to ~0.2 V below Vth and back in 2 ns; each access transistor's gate charge depends weakly on its storage-node (source) voltage through the body effect, so a per-driver charge integrator measures the row's '1'-count without any charge transfer. A 10-bit popcount tag written with the row is compared and a mismatch triggers a targeted scrub.
why: Row hammer and refresh tail (facts 3, 9): row-level corruption is detected for ~1/100 of an activation's energy, enabling detection-driven rather than worst-case protective refresh; claimed 5-10x fewer mitigation refreshes.

title: Buried bitline's own junction becomes a millimeter-scale JFET preamp
idea: Stack: cut sense-amp offset 5x AND add no area at bitline pitch. In 4F2 vertical-channel DRAM with buried n+ bitlines, implant a lightly doped p-strip beside each bitline under the array, contacted only at the mat edges; the bitline's depletion edge modulates the strip's conductance along its whole length, so the parasitic bitline-to-substrate capacitance doubles as the gate of a giant-area JFET. True and reference strips form a differential current preamp ahead of a small latch.
why: Sensing and periphery area (facts 1, 7): mismatch scales as 1/sqrt(gate area), so a 50-100 um gate gives sub-mV offset and lets each sense amp serve ~2x more cells (~10% die area).

title: Per-die ECC-aware address permutation key replaces redundancy and fuses
idea: Stack: at most 8 bits of repair storage AND zero spare rows or columns. At sort the tester maps defects and searches 256 hard-wired XOR/rotate column-to-codeword permutations for one that puts no more than one defective cell in any on-die-ECC codeword; the 8-bit key is loaded from the SPD into a mode register, and on-die SEC silently absorbs the steered defects.
why: Periphery area and test cost (fact 7): deletes redundant rows/columns, fuse banks and compare logic (~4-6% of die) in exchange for an 8-bit key; ECC headroom is lost only in the few defect-hosting words.

title: High-equalized bitlines collect hammer electrons as the aggressor wordline falls
idea: Stack: no activation counters AND no extra refresh. Reorder precharge so that during the ~2 ns in which the aggressor wordline falls, every bitline in the mat is held at VDD instead of being equalized to VDD/2; electrons detrapped from the aggressor's gate-edge and STI interface traps then drift into the nearby positively biased bitline-contact junctions rather than the victims' storage nodes, and normal equalization follows.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): attacks the charge-pumping injection mechanism at its source with only a timing change; claimed 3-10x higher hammer threshold, so tracker tables shrink or disappear.

title: ACT-timed feed-forward charge packets replace on-die decoupling capacitors
idea: Stack: cut decap area 70% AND keep VARY droop unchanged. The command decoder knows the exact cycle each bank's sense amps fire, so a per-bank reservoir capacitor held at 2.5 V dumps a calibrated charge packet into the local VARY grid through a timed switch at that instant, cancelling droop actively; packet size is trimmed per bank from an on-die droop monitor.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): activation decap is several percent of die; a 2.5x voltage swing on a small reservoir delivers the same charge from ~1/5 of the capacitance.

title: Segmented spare rows: one spare row patches eight defective rows
idea: Stack: 75% fewer spare rows AND the same repairable defect count. Split each spare row along the existing sub-wordline-driver boundaries into eight independently remappable segments, each with its own small address match, so one physical spare row stands in for the local defective segment of up to eight different rows, since point defects rarely span a full row.
why: Redundancy share of periphery (fact 7): spare rows plus their fuses and comparators are ~2-3% of die; segment-granular sparing recovers most of it.

title: TSV copper gates an annular power transistor inside its keep-out zone
idea: Stack: use no silicon outside the TSV keep-out ring AND add bank power gating. A dedicated gate TSV runs through the stack; its liner oxide serves as the gate dielectric of a ring-shaped gate-all-around MOSFET formed by implanting source/drain rings in the otherwise dead keep-out silicon, so one TSV drive power-gates the same bank on every die of an HBM stack at once.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and idle power: turns dead keep-out area (~10% of an HBM core die) into power switches; ~100 ns gating speed is adequate for bank-level idle.

title: Open-row delta parity update removes on-die ECC read-modify-write
idea: Stack: keep on-die ECC AND never do an internal read-modify-write for masked or partial writes. With the row open, the old codeword already sits in the sense-amp latches, so a small XOR tree in the column path computes the parity change from only the overwritten bits (old XOR new) and flips the parity columns of the same open row directly in their latches within the same column cycle.
why: Bandwidth and periphery energy: DDR5 masked writes cost an extra internal column read; delta update removes it, worth ~10-20% effective write bandwidth on partial-write workloads.

title: Cell plate electrode doubles as a low-swing mat broadcast wire
idea: Stack: delete a global control-wire bundle AND add no metal. The cell plate of each mat is driven with +/-50 mV coded pulses (mat select, sense-enable timing tokens) that small comparators in the sub-wordline-driver strips decode; storage nodes are capacitively tied to the plate and simply ride along, so stored charge relative to the plate is unchanged.
why: Periphery wiring (fact 7): turns an always-present low-resistance conductor into a signal path, freeing ~5-10% of upper-metal tracks in conjunction areas.

title: Flip-minimizing write inversion for writes into an already-open row
idea: Stack: cut row-buffer write energy AND leave the external bus untouched. For each write burst into an open row, the column logic compares new data with the latched old data and stores the inverted word plus a 1-bit flag whenever that flips fewer sense-amp latches; the flag cell lives in the same row and is applied on read.
why: Energy per bit: each flipped latch swings two bitline capacitances rail to rail; inversion caps flips per word below half, trimming write restore energy ~20-30%.

title: Clocked MIM switched-capacitor resistor replaces the external ZQ resistor
idea: Stack: no precision external resistor or ZQ pin AND +/-5% driver impedance. A switched-capacitor equivalent resistor R = 1/(f*C), built from an on-die MIM capacitor clocked by CK, becomes the impedance reference; the MIM value is trimmed once at sort and tracked by the host-controlled clock frequency.
why: Periphery and package cost: removes a pin, a board component per die and the ZQ arbitration logic, which matters most in many-die stacks.

title: Stack-shared ESD lets HBM core dies drop per-TSV clamps
idea: Stack: keep handling ESD robustness AND remove full clamps from every core-die TSV I/O. Core dies carry only a tiny CDM-level clamp per TSV and are assembled with a sacrificial laser-opened shunt layer shorting all TSV columns; after bonding, the base die's full clamps protect each vertical column for every die.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): per-TSV ESD devices and their spacing are a notable slice of ~2000 TSV I/O sites per core die; dropping them reclaims area and cuts TSV load capacitance ~30%.

title: Delta-coded trims: mask-ROM baseline plus tiny per-die fuse deltas
idea: Stack: shrink the fuse bank 4x AND keep per-die trims. Hard-code the product-median value of every trim (VPP, VARY, timing, references) in mask ROM and store per die only small signed deltas in a variable-length code; the boot loader adds them, since most dies sit near the median.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): e-fuse arrays and their sense latches take ~1-2% of die; entropy-coding the trims shrinks them several-fold.

title: GHz-clocked micro charge pumps embedded in every sub-wordline-driver strip
idea: Stack: no central VPP pump block AND no off-die supply. Replace the ~100 MHz central pump with hundreds of two-stage micro-pumps clocked at 2-4 GHz from the I/O clock, each with 5-10 pF of BEOL MIM inside the driver strip it feeds; flying-cap area scales as 1/f and local generation deletes the VPP distribution mesh.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): VPP pumps and capacitors are ~3-5% of die; 20x higher clocking cuts capacitor area ~10x at a modest efficiency cost.

title: Predicted mats pre-bias their wordlines just below threshold
idea: Stack: cut wordline activation charge 40% AND keep tRCD. When the scheduler queues an ACT for a mat, that mat's wordlines are lifted from the negative off level to ~0.3 V below Vth for at most 50 ns, shrinking the boosted swing the selected row and its driver must deliver; unselected rows return negative long before extra leakage matters.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): VPP charge is produced at ~30% pump efficiency, so a 40% smaller boosted swing saves ~10-15% of activate power.

title: In-DRAM row copy fills retention-test patterns in microseconds
idea: Stack: halve retention-test cost AND buy no new testers. A test mode lets the tester write one pattern row per subarray, then the die replicates it into every row by back-to-back activation copy and inverts it with a broadcast flag, collapsing each pattern fill from milliseconds over the narrow test bus to microseconds.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): multi-pattern retention tests dominate DRAM test time and tester capex; faster fills roughly double tester throughput.

title: Contact-over-active-gate layout shrinks sense-amp strip height
idea: Stack: shrink sense-amp strips 15% AND keep transistor sizes. Bring the logic-node contact-over-active-gate scheme to the sense-amp and equalizer layout: gate contacts land directly above the channel through a self-aligned cap, so the cross-coupled pair no longer needs gate extensions beyond the active area for contacts.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-amp strips are ~15-20% of die; removing gate-extension real estate cuts strip height ~10-15%.

title: One time-shared bank decoder serves row and column addresses
idea: Stack: halve decode transistor count AND keep random access. ACT and READ/WRITE to a bank are always separated by tRCD (>10 ns), so a single bank decoder decodes the row address, latches the one-hot result into sub-wordline-driver keepers, and is then reused for the column address with outputs steered to the column-select drivers.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): row plus column decoders are ~5-8% of die; time-sharing removes most of one of them.

title: Self-clocked single-wire internal command bus replaces parallel control routing
idea: Stack: cut bank control wiring 10x AND add no command latency beyond one cycle. Each bank's internal commands and addresses travel as a Manchester-coded serial stream on one wire at 8x the internal clock, recovered by a tiny edge-detecting deserializer at the bank, instead of dozens of parallel control and predecode lines crossing the die.
why: Periphery wiring (fact 7): control and address buses consume a large share of upper-metal tracks in the central spine; serializing them frees area and reduces switching capacitance.

title: Internal global data lines carry reads and writes simultaneously
idea: Stack: halve global data-line count AND keep read-write turnaround at zero. Each internal GIO wire is driven from both ends at once (array side for reads, I/O side for writes) and each end's receiver subtracts its own known transmitted level through a replica hybrid, so a bank streams reads outward while the next writes flow inward.
why: Periphery wiring and bandwidth (fact 7): global data lines occupy many upper-metal tracks; simultaneous bidirectional signaling halves them.

title: Voltage-ratio steering writes sub-pitch bits into a continuous ferroelectric film
idea: Collision: zero refresh demands a remanent medium, while 10x density at flat cost forbids 10x finer lithography. Keep a continuous HZO film and coarse 40 nm electrodes, and let periphery DACs set the voltage ratio on four neighbouring electrodes so the coercive-field maximum lands on any of 4x4 sub-pitch spots that a square-loop film switches alone. Reads apply the same steered field, sense the switching charge on the shared electrodes and rewrite.
why: Litho capital and refresh (facts 3, 4): 16 bits per coarse cell from electrode DACs instead of EUV; nonvolatile, so zero refresh; claimed ~10x bits per mask level.

title: Row-line Joule heating plus column field selects Curie-edge ferroelectric bits
idea: Collision: no refresh needs a remanent dipole, and flat-cost 10x density allows no access transistor. Use a ferroelectric engineered with a Curie point near 150 C, where its coercive field collapses: a 5 ns current pulse heats one row line, and only cells on that hot row switch under the moderate column voltage while cold rows ignore it. Eight such decks stack in BEOL with drivers only at tile edges.
why: Deletes access transistors and selectors (facts 2, 4): ~4F2/8 per bit with thermal coincidence replacing V/2 schemes; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Nanosecond write pulses exploit ferroelectric switching kinetics against half-select
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to ferroelectric storage, and 10x density at flat cost points to selector-free crosspoints that normally die of half-select disturb. Switching time follows Merz's law t ~ exp(alpha/E), so a 1 ns full-field pulse switches the target while half-field cells would need ~1e9x longer; drivers with sub-100 ps edges and regulated amplitude enforce the window, and a per-line disturb counter triggers rare rewrites.
why: Transistor-free FE crosspoint decks (facts 2, 4): density from 4F2 times decks with edge-only drivers; nonvolatile.

title: Sneak current through the crosspoint becomes the read reference
idea: Collision: zero refresh forces two-terminal nonvolatile cells, and flat-cost 10x density forbids per-cell selectors, so sneak paths are unavoidable. Use them as the reference: with balanced-coded data the sneak current through all unselected three-cell paths is a stable multiple of the mean cell conductance, so each column sense amp compares the selected cell's current against a scaled copy of the measured sneak current instead of a reference column.
why: Sensing in selectorless arrays (fact 7): deletes reference columns and tracks drift and temperature, enabling ~1k x 1k tiles; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Magnetoelectric bits flip only where line voltage meets package coil field
idea: Collision: no refresh calls for a magnetic state, and flat-cost density calls for no write transistors or currents. Cr2O3-type magnetoelectric antiferromagnets switch only when the product of electric and magnetic field crosses a threshold, so one package-level coil supplies a global +/-H pulse while row and column lines apply +/-V/2 and only the crossing sees the full E*H product. Reads use the exchange-coupled ferromagnet's anomalous Hall voltage on the same lines.
why: Write drivers shrink to voltage switches with no current (fact 7); crosspoint decks provide the density; nonvolatile.

title: Ultrasonic echo timing reads a whole ferroelectric row from one transducer
idea: Collision: zero refresh means remanent polarization, and 10x density means no per-column sense amp. A sub-coercive voltage step on one row makes each cell launch a piezoelectric acoustic wavelet whose phase follows its polarization sign; a single AlN transducer at the tile edge receives them in time-of-flight order (~5 um/ns), so column position becomes arrival time and one receiver decodes a 50 um row in ~10 ns without switching any cell.
why: Periphery area and destructive read (facts 7, 8): one receiver replaces hundreds of sense amps, reads are non-destructive and storage is nonvolatile.

title: Coulomb-metered write termination stretches ferroelectric endurance toward unlimited
idea: Collision: zero refresh chooses ferroelectric storage, but 10x density at the same cost leaves no spare cells to mask fatigue. Each plate or bitline driver integrates the switching current and ends the write pulse the moment 2Pr*A of charge has moved, so no cell ever sees excess field or time, the main driver of oxygen-vacancy fatigue and imprint; cells needing abnormal charge are flagged early.
why: DRAM-class endurance in dense FE decks: removing overdrive extends cycling ~10-100x, letting 3D ferroelectric capacitors serve as working memory; nonvolatile.

title: Idle-time rejuvenation pulses reset ferroelectric fatigue tile by tile
idea: Collision: zero refresh still leaves energy for rare maintenance, while flat-cost 10x density forbids over-provisioning cells. Each tile logs its write count; during idle windows the periphery moves the tile's data to a spare tile, applies a short burst of high-field bipolar cycles that redistributes oxygen vacancies and restores remanent polarization, then moves the data back.
why: Endurance at density: in-situ fatigue recovery turns a ~1e11-cycle ferroelectric into an effectively unlimited one; nonvolatile, no refresh.

title: Antiferroelectric layers act as capacitive tier selectors in 3D ferroelectric stacks
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric storage capacitors, and 10x density at flat cost means many tiers on one vertical bitline without a transistor per tier. Put a ZrO2 antiferroelectric capacitor in series with each tier's storage capacitor: unbiased it is a small linear capacitance that blocks charge transfer, but when the tier's plate drives it past its AFE-to-FE field its capacitance jumps ~5x and couples that storage cell to the bitline.
why: Deletes per-tier access transistors and staircase decoders (facts 2, 7): capacitive selection lets 32+ tiers share one bitline; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Binary-weighted stray fields let one sensor junction read four magnets
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to nanomagnets, and 10x density points to fewer read devices than bits. Place four unwired storage nanomagnets at engineered distances above one sensor MTJ so their stray fields at the sensor are weighted 1:2:4:8; the sensor's resistance encodes all four states in one read through a 4-bit current ADC, while writes use one shared spin-orbit line per stack.
why: Read periphery and access devices per bit drop 4x (fact 7); storage magnets need no transistor or contact; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Sliding-ferroelectric bilayer gates switch at 0.3 V and delete charge pumps
idea: Collision: zero refresh requires remanence, and 10x density at the same cost requires the periphery to shrink rather than grow. Use rhombohedral bilayer MoS2 or hBN, whose polarization flips by interlayer sliding at ~0.3 V without domain-pinning fatigue, as the storage gate of a 2D-channel read transistor; with sub-0.5 V writes the periphery needs no VPP pumps, level shifters or thick-oxide drivers, and transferred 2D tiers stack.
why: Voltage floor and periphery area (facts 7, 10): deleting high-voltage periphery frees ~15% of die and thin tiers stack; nonvolatile.

title: Pre-poled spare rows make every ferroelectric write one-directional
idea: Collision: zero refresh chooses ferroelectric storage, and flat-cost density chooses cheap crosspoint decks whose endurance is the weak point. The periphery keeps a pool of rows pre-poled to '0' by row-parallel plate pulses in idle time; every write goes out of place to such a row so only the '1' bits switch, and a remap table in the sense-amp strip sends the old row back to the pre-pole queue.
why: Halves switching events and write energy, removes read-before-write and doubles write speed in dense nonvolatile decks.

title: Reprogrammable ferroelectric capacitive decoders built inside the storage deck
idea: Collision: zero refresh plus flat-cost 10x density leaves no budget for CMOS decoders per deck. Build each deck's row decoder from the same ferroelectric capacitors as its cells: an address-line by row-line capacitor matrix whose polarization pattern decides which address combination couples enough charge to push a row line past its threshold-switch selector; the pattern is written at test and rewritten in the field to map out bad rows.
why: Periphery area and masks (facts 4, 7): decoders come free with the deck process and double as repair; nonvolatile.

title: Write-credit protocol trades write speed for 10x denser nonvolatile tiers
idea: Collision: zero refresh and flat-cost 10x density point to dense ferroelectric or magnetic crosspoints whose writes are slower than reads. The periphery advertises a per-bank write-credit pool over CXL; hosts spend a credit per line written and credits refill at the array's sustainable rate while reads stay DRAM-fast, so read-heavy inference (weights, KV cache) uses dense memory without a DRAM write cache.
why: Lets accelerators adopt 10x-density, zero-refresh tiers under an explicit contract instead of paying for an extra DRAM front end.

title: Polarization-vector cells store two bits read by orthogonal electrode pairs
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric remanence, and 10x density at flat cost means more bits per lithographic cell. In rhombohedral BiFeO3 the polarization takes four projected diagonal orientations, so each crosspoint gets a vertical electrode pair and a lateral electrode pair; the vertical component is read by one pair and the in-plane component by the other, giving 2 bits per cell from two binary reads rather than multilevel sensing.
why: Doubles bits per cell without analog levels; with crosspoint decks reaches 10x density; nonvolatile.

title: Mirror-poled alternate decks share lines without write disturb
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric decks, and 10x density means decks must share word and bit lines. Deposit every other deck with its electrode stack mirrored so its ferroelectric imprint points the opposite way: a write field that switches the target in deck k only pushes the sharing deck's cells further into saturation, and read pulses of opposite polarity address the upper or lower deck through the same sense amp.
why: Halves line layers and drivers per deck (facts 4, 7) while removing shared-line disturb; nonvolatile, zero refresh.

title: Global microwave plus local voltage tuning writes magnetic crosspoint bits
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to nanomagnets, and flat-cost density points to no write transistors and no write currents. A package stripline bathes the die in a GHz field slightly off the bits' ferromagnetic resonance; the row-column voltage at one crossing shifts that bit's anisotropy through voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy into resonance, so only it absorbs enough energy to reverse.
why: Write drivers become current-free voltage switches (fact 7); crosspoint decks provide density; nonvolatile.

title: Abort-on-nucleation sensing reads ferroelectric cells without full switching
idea: Collision: zero refresh chooses ferroelectric cells, and 10x density forbids spending energy and endurance on full destructive reads. The sense amp watches displacement current during a read ramp and kills the ramp within ~100 ps of the first switching-current onset, so a '1' cell is only nucleated, not switched, and back-switches when the field is removed; the onset itself is the data.
why: Destructive read (fact 8) and endurance: roughly halves read fatigue and removes most write-back energy; nonvolatile.

title: Balanced-coded rows cancel plate switching current and shrink plate drivers
idea: Collision: zero refresh means ferroelectric switching charge on every write, and 10x density at the same cost means plate drivers cannot grow with bits per row. Encode each row with a constant-weight code and write '1's and '0's in one pulse so up- and down-switching displacement currents cancel on the shared plate; the plate driver supplies only the imbalance and the linear charge.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): plate and word drivers shrink ~5-10x, the key enabler for long FE crosspoint lines; nonvolatile.

title: Compensating reverse pulses undo partial switching in half-selected cells
idea: Collision: zero refresh plus flat-cost density forces selectorless ferroelectric crosspoints, whose half-selected cells partially switch on every write. The line drivers follow each write with a short opposite-polarity half-amplitude pulse on the shared lines only, reversing sub-critical nuclei in half-selected cells while being far too weak to disturb the fully switched target.
why: Removes the half-select disturb barrier that has blocked transistor-free ferroelectric arrays since 1952, enabling dense decks; nonvolatile.

title: Anomalous Nernst readout heats one row and reads magnets as voltages
idea: Collision: zero refresh points to magnetic bits, and 10x density at the same cost forbids a tunnel junction and transistor per bit. Each bit is a nanomagnet with a Nernst-active layer (for example Co2MnGa) between a row heater line and a column sense line; a 2 ns heat pulse on one row produces a transverse anomalous Nernst voltage at each crossing whose sign gives the magnetization, read by column comparators.
why: Transistor-free, junction-free magnetic crosspoints (facts 2, 7); nonvolatile; the read path is only heaters and comparators.
